doc.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012

title: Whether filmmakers need film school
summary: Crohn discusses film school contacts versus learning on your own, his comparative literature degree and slide-and-beep film strips.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Nowadays we can talk about jazz education, we can have the same conversation about film education. Do people need to go to film school?

You know these days, because people are so computer literate and so many programs make it easy to do anything, I think kids come out of grade school or out of secondary school, if they have any interest in video at all they can do digital editing, they’ve shot on cameras. I mean I think if you want to go make feature films there’s two reasons to go to film schools. You do learn a lot and you get a lot of hands-on experience, and you make great contacts. You work on other people’s films, they work on yours, and when the time comes when the people get a Hollywood contract they call their friends to work on the film. I never was good in school at anything. I always had to learn my own way.
Comparative literature — with a minor in psychology.
I like — you used the term “film strips” I can remember the beep — turn the dial.
Exactly. And after a while they became automated to the beep would activate the slide projector.
